newsitem.title: UK: Strong sterling to keep UK rates low after election.
newsitem.headline: Strong sterling to keep UK rates low after election.

text.p: Whichever party wins Britain's forthcoming election, the pound's brisk rise on world markets over the past year will allow them to keep interest rates at historically low levels, economists said on Monday.

And if, as widely expected, Labour wins the next election which must be held by May and Gordon Brown becomes Chancellor of the Exchequer, he will find the pound's rally presents a problem laced with both opportunity and danger.

"Brown could find sterling's rally, if unchecked, could cause real problems by making our exports more expensive still and pushing industry into recession," said Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets.

While a strong pound makes it harder for British exporters to sell their goods, it also cuts down the real cost of imported raw materials and energy goods to Britain, which helps companies keep their prices, and inflation generally, low.

British industry is already squealing as the pound has rallied some 16 percent against major trading currencies since August, and there is concern that Labour's more Euro-friendly attitude could encourage a further rally after the election.
But sterling's strength has a silver lining for Labour, which has been out of power since 1979 and has been damaged by a reputation for poor economic management.

"The rise in the currency will help keep inflation under control so interest rates will not have to rise sharply. Also, it will give Brown a chance to tighten fiscal policy quickly in a mini-budget to re-balance the economy," Loynes said.

Loynes said Brown could use the mini-budget to tighten fiscal policy by around four billion pounds ($6.5 billion) in fiscal 1997-8, which would help slow rising consumer spending (through back-door tax increases such as restricting tax allowances), and cut a budget debt bill which remains stubbornly high despite four consecutive years of perky economic growth.
More important, it would allow fiscal rather than monetary policy to take the strain on keeping inflation in check, and stop the pound rallying too far on world markets.
Economists said sterling's strength and low inflation will allow Labour to only raise interest rates modestly -- a relief to many in a country where 67 percent borrow money to buy their own homes.
"We will see just two quarter point rises in interest rates after the election, whichever party wins power," said Jeremy Hawkins, economist at Bank America.
"With base lending rates currently at six percent, that represents a very modest tightening in keeping with the underlying committment to fine-tune monetary policy adjustments."

Many economists believe that interest rates will stay relatively low -- at least by historic if not international standards -- in 1997 and 1998, allowing Labour to finally shed its reputation as a high-inflation, high interest rate party.

"Inflation will stay low with the core measure of inflation at around 2.8 percent by the end of this year and falling to the target of 2.5 percent by the end of 1998. In these circumstances, I see interest rates at 6.75 percent by the end of 1997 and falling to 6.5 percent by the end of 1998," said economist Hawkins.
Michael Saunders, economist at Salomon Brothers, agrees.

"We see a total hike in interest rates of 0.5 percentage point after the election, assuming that sterling stays around current levels. Base rates are likely to level off and stay below seven percent next year," he said.
The pound stood at 1.6280 dollars and 2.7240 marks at around 1400 gmt.
